source: DMZ Scuba site research: facts cross-checked against the cited agency and archaeological records; summaries written by DMZ Scuba.

lake-michigan.name: Lake Michigan
notes: Summer brings a thermocline: below it, expect 40–45°F water even when the surface is warm.
Invasive quagga and zebra mussels coat most wrecks and keep the water unusually clear.
Fresh water: you need less weight than in the sea.

whs.name: Wisconsin Shipwrecks — Wisconsin Historical Society & Wisconsin Sea Grant

nps.name: National Park Service — Sleeping Bear Dunes shipwrecks

geonames-gilboa-fixture-2564638.name: Gilboa Quarry
geonames-gilboa-fixture-2564638.access: Private quarry; deep side requires certification or an instructor
highlights: Sunken planes and helicopters
Nemo's Garden underwater biosphere
geonames-gilboa-fixture-2564638.summary: A spring-fed former limestone quarry west of Findlay, Ohio, popular for training and deep diving. It has sunken aircraft and vehicles and clear water, with a deep side to about 137-140 ft.

noaa-fknms-adelaide-baker.name: Adelaide Baker
highlights: Iron mast and hull remains with gorgonians and sponges
noaa-fknms-adelaide-baker.summary: The scattered remains of a three-masted sailing ship wrecked in 1889, lying in about 20 feet near Duck Key and covered with sponges, gorgonians and corals.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-adolphus-busch-wreck.name: Adolphus Busch Wreck
noaa-fknms-adolphus-busch-wreck.summary: A 210-foot freighter standing upright on sand near Looe Key in the Lower Keys, sunk in 1998 as an artificial reef and now part of the Florida Keys shipwreck trail.
sources: Florida Keys & Key West tourism council

noaa-fknms-alligator-reef.name: Alligator Reef
highlights: Historic lighthouse marks the reef
Over 600 reef fish species recorded
noaa-fknms-alligator-reef.summary: A shallow protected bank reef off the Alligator lighthouse, with spur-and-groove coral and a big fish list. Calm depths make it a good fit for newer divers and snorkelers.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-amesbury-wreck.name: Amesbury Wreck
highlights: Two hull sections 600 ft apart with 5-inch gun mount
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary
NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-benwood-wreck.name: Benwood Wreck
highlights: Intact bow rising about 25 ft off the bottom
Resident porkfish, goatfish and schoolmaster snapper
noaa-fknms-benwood-wreck.summary: A freighter lost in 1942 and now a Florida Keys Shipwreck Trail dive off Key Largo, lying in 25-45 ft among low reef and sand. The bow is the most complete section, and schooling snapper and porkfish make it a popular, comfortable wreck dive.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-bibb-wreck.name: Bibb Wreck
hazards: Current can make the wreck undiveable at times
noaa-fknms-bibb-wreck.summary: The Duane's sister cutter, lying on its side in deeper water off Key Largo. It is a deeper, advanced dive, and current can shut it down on some days.

noaa-fknms-duane-wreck.name: Duane Wreck
noaa-fknms-duane-wreck.depthNote: Mast 60 ft, bridge 70 ft, main deck 100 ft, sand 120 ft
highlights: Intact upright cutter with rails, ladders and props
Multilevel dive from mast down to main deck
hazards: Gulf Stream current can be fierce at times
noaa-fknms-duane-wreck.summary: A 327-foot Coast Guard cutter sitting upright on sand near Molasses Reef, with the mast near 60 feet and decks stepping down to 120. Currents can run hard, but it makes an easy multilevel wreck dive.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-eagle-wreck.name: Eagle Wreck
noaa-fknms-eagle-wreck.depthNote: Rails 70 ft, prop and rudder 110 ft
highlights: Goliath groupers and bull sharks
Schooling jacks around the hull
Propeller and rudder still intact
hazards: Wreck broken in half by Hurricane Georges
noaa-fknms-eagle-wreck.summary: A 287-foot freighter resting on its starboard side off Islamorada, with rails near 70 feet and propeller at 110. Big groupers, bull sharks and jacks circle the wreck.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-eastern-dry-rocks.name: Eastern Dry Rocks
highlights: Coral fingers and sand-floored canyons
noaa-fknms-eastern-dry-rocks.summary: A small bank reef near Key West packing several reef habitats into about 90 acres, with rubble, coral ridges and sandy canyons in shallow water.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-grecian-rocks.name: Grecian Rocks
highlights: Purple fan corals swaying in the current
noaa-fknms-grecian-rocks.summary: A shallow patch reef off Key Largo beside the Christ of the Abyss site, whose crest breaks the surface at high tide. It is sheltered enough to dive or snorkel on breezy days and is rich in fan corals and reef fish.

noaa-fknms-joe-s-tug-wreck.name: Joe's Tug Wreck
highlights: Moray eels and schools of fish in the hull
Resident goliath grouper known as Elvis
noaa-fknms-joe-s-tug-wreck.summary: A 75-foot steel shrimp boat, not a tug, lying in two halves in about 65 feet off Key West. A popular novice wreck with schooling fish, morays and often excellent visibility.

noaa-fknms-looe-key.name: Looe Key
noaa-fknms-looe-key.access: Sanctuary Preservation Area with special regulations; boat only
noaa-fknms-looe-key.summary: A spur-and-groove coral reef about six miles offshore of Ramrod and Big Pine Keys, protected as a sanctuary preservation area. Shallow coral fingers and sand channels hold reef sharks, rays and groupers.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-molasses-reef.name: Molasses Reef
highlights: Boulder corals on a spur-and-groove outer reef
Ship's winch and old Spanish anchor on the bottom
noaa-fknms-molasses-reef.summary: Key Largo's busiest outer reef, with spur-and-groove coral, big boulder corals and plentiful fish. Water is often clear, and a winch and an old anchor lie off the lighthouse.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-newfound-harbor.name: Newfound Harbor
highlights: Boulder, star and giant brain corals
noaa-fknms-newfound-harbor.summary: A shallow inshore patch reef off Little Palm Island with large boulder, star and brain corals and reef fish, all within 18 feet of the surface.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-north-dry-rocks.name: North Dry Rocks
highlights: Coral mounds with abundant tropical fish

noaa-fknms-pickles-reef.name: Pickles Reef
highlights: Juvenile nurse sharks and stingrays in sand channels
Remains of the Pickle Barrel civil-war era wreck
noaa-fknms-pickles-reef.summary: A shallow spur-and-groove reef off Key Largo with barrel-shaped coral heads, easy navigation and sea fans. Gentle depths suit new divers and snorkelers, and small fish make it a good photo site.

noaa-fknms-rock-key.name: Rock Key
highlights: Coral fingers and sand-floored canyons
noaa-fknms-rock-key.summary: A bank reef off Key West made up of a rubble zone, long coral fingers and sandy, coral-lined canyons, in water shallow enough for relaxed dives.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-san-pedro-wreck.name: San Pedro Wreck
noaa-fknms-san-pedro-wreck.access: State of Florida Underwater Archaeological Preserve
highlights: Ballast pile of a 1733 Spanish fleet wreck
noaa-fknms-san-pedro-wreck.summary: The ballast mound of a Spanish ship lost in the 1733 hurricane, resting in about 18 feet south of Indian Key. It is a protected state archaeological preserve.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-sand-key-reef.name: Sand Key Reef
highlights: Spur-and-groove reef beside a 1853 iron lighthouse
hazards: Fire coral common on sections of the reef
noaa-fknms-sand-key-reef.summary: A spur-and-groove reef seven miles off Key West, topped by a historic red iron lighthouse. Coral ridges rise in shallow water and the south side slopes off to a deeper ledge; visibility swings widely with wind and tide.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-snapper-ledge.name: Snapper Ledge
highlights: Huge boulder brain coral
Yellowtail snapper, nurse sharks, morays
noaa-fknms-snapper-ledge.summary: A shallow Key Largo ledge reef suited to open-water divers, known for a very large boulder brain coral and schools of snapper with nurse sharks and morays around.

noaa-fknms-sombrero-reef.name: Sombrero Reef
highlights: Classic spur-and-groove reef formation
noaa-fknms-sombrero-reef.summary: A large spur-and-groove reef in the Middle Keys, shallower than 30 feet inside its protected zone and a favourite for both snorkelers and divers.
sources: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary

noaa-fknms-spiegel-grove-wreck.name: Spiegel Grove Wreck
highlights: Huge wreck: one dive covers only a fraction of it
hazards: Silt-outs inside the hull cause disorientation
Overhead environment beyond ambient light
noaa-fknms-spiegel-grove-wreck.summary: A 510-ft Navy landing ship dock sunk off Key Largo as an artificial reef, with its top deck near 60 ft and hull to about 135 ft. Its sheer size rewards repeat dives, but depth and a silt-prone interior make it an advanced-diver wreck.

noaa-fknms-vandenberg-wreck.name: Vandenberg Wreck
noaa-fknms-vandenberg-wreck.depthNote: Superstructure 45 ft, hull on sand about 145 ft
highlights: About 100 ft of vertical relief
noaa-fknms-vandenberg-wreck.summary: A 523-foot former missile-tracking ship sunk off Key West, one of the largest purpose-sunk wrecks anywhere. Its hull sits at about 145 feet while the top reaches 45 feet, so there is a profile for most divers.
sources: Florida Keys & Key West tourism council

odm-6zgdzb.name: Crystal Bay, Nusa Penida
highlights: Mola mola (ocean sunfish) in the cooler months
hazards: Currents can be very strong
odm-6zgdzb.summary: A sheltered bay off Nusa Penida with some of Bali's clearest water, divable in the bay or around the small island offshore. Ocean sunfish visit in the cooler months, but currents outside the bay demand experience.

odm-b4trti.name: Manta Ray Heaven, Garden Eel Cove
highlights: Night manta ray feeding under dive lights
Garden eels on the sandy bottom
hazards: Exposed to open ocean; boat ride can be choppy
odm-b4trti.summary: A coral shelf in Makako Bay off Kona airport that is a day site for garden eels and, at night, the Big Island's manta ray dive. Operators run boat trips; divers kneel on sand at about 35 feet while mantas feed on plankton.

odm-hz36jx.name: Black Rock - Hawaii
highlights: Green sea turtles and night-time eels, lobsters, reef squid
odm-hz36jx.summary: Black Rock (Pu'u Keka'a) at Ka'anapali is an easy beach-entry dive along a rocky ledge reaching about 30 feet. Suited to beginners, with turtles by day and octopus, eels and squid at night.

odm-qmjree.name: Pink Beach Komodo
highlights: Pygmy seahorses on sea fans
Hawksbill turtles feeding on sponges
odm-qmjree.summary: A calm, sheltered coral slope on Komodo's coast, shallow and gentle enough for newly certified divers. It makes a relaxed break between Komodo's current-swept dives, with good macro life and turtles.

odm-tb91a5.name: Ulua Beach Park
highlights: Turtle cleaning station on the second reef
odm-tb91a5.summary: A beach-entry reef dive in Wailea, South Maui, used for scuba instruction thanks to gentle conditions and a gradual slope. Turtles visit a cleaning station on the second reef; swells can ruin visibility.

odm-wrndzo.name: Siaba Besar
highlights: Green turtles ('Turtle City')
Macro life on sandy patches
odm-wrndzo.summary: A sheltered bay in central Komodo National Park with coral bommies and sandy patches on a gentle slope. Calm and shallow, it is known for its resident turtles and is popular for first and check-out dives.

odm-zvbfl0.name: Salem Express, wreck
odm-zvbfl0.penetration: Penetration frowned upon; many guides refuse as it is a maritime grave
highlights: Two giant propellers and rudder
Personal items still lie on the seabed
hazards: Currents can be strong
Memorial wreck; many guides will not dive it
odm-zvbfl0.summary: A ferry lost in 1991 near Safaga, now on her side on sand with her highest point near 7 m and her deepest about 27 to 30 m. A sombre, advanced boat dive on a grave site, where penetration is discouraged.

osm-n12601944496.name: Lofthus
osm-n12601944496.access: Florida Underwater Archaeological Preserve, open free year-round; anchor in sand
hazards: Sand movement buries or exposes parts of the wreck
osm-n12601944496.summary: An 1898 iron barque wrecked and later blasted, leaving a scattered wreck site just off Manalapan near Boynton Beach in about 15 to 20 feet. It is a state archaeological preserve suited to snorkelers and new divers.

osm-n1485422409.name: Pantai Merah
osm-n1485422409.depthNote: Sources also call Pantai Merah Pink Beach.
highlights: Healthy coral garden, turtles, whitetip reef sharks

osm-n2171849465.name: Glenlyon
osm-n2171849465.summary: A steel package freighter wrecked on Isle Royale's Glenlyon Shoals in 1924. The cold lake has preserved the bow, engine room and cabin in shallow water, and the open-to-the-public wreck is far less visited than other park wrecks.

osm-n255316037.name: SS Thistlegorm
osm-n255316037.penetration: Holds 1 to 3 can be swum through at up to 25 m
highlights: BSA motorbikes, trucks and cars in the holds
Ship largely intact, upright on sand
hazards: Currents can be strong
osm-n255316037.summary: A British freighter bombed in 1941 and now sitting upright on sand at about 30 m in the Gulf of Suez, with her wartime cargo of vehicles and motorbikes still stowed in the holds. A deep, advanced boat dive.

osm-n2628832137.name: Laguna Reef
hazards: Strong tidal flows dictate the dive plan
osm-n2628832137.summary: A shallow hard-coral lagoon on the west of Tiran island, split in two by a coral wall into North and South Laguna, with a drift along the outer wall suited to all levels. Tidal flow controls when and how it is dived.

osm-n270804074.name: Richelieu Rock
osm-n270804074.access: Inside Surin Islands National Park; open only in the dry season
highlights: Whale sharks and mantas, Feb-Apr
Harlequin shrimp under overhangs
Schools of barracuda and mackerel
hazards: Currents can strengthen mid-dive around the horseshoe
osm-n270804074.summary: Isolated horseshoe-shaped pinnacle in Mu Ko Surin National Park, rising from about 35 m to just below the surface. Famed for purple soft corals, macro life and occasional whale sharks; currents can be strong and the park is open only in the dry season.

osm-n271181711.name: The Bells
highlights: Chimney descent lit by sun rays
Cleaner fish station at about 18 m
hazards: Narrow chimney entry; mini arch at 26 m is not the Arch
osm-n271181711.summary: A shore entry through a narrow reef chimney that exits onto a wall at about 26-28 m, then follows the wall to the saddle into the Blue Hole. Guided centres take qualified divers to 30 m.

osm-n3149301713.name: Weeki Wachee Spring
osm-n3149301713.depthNote: Cave-system maximum, not a normal open-water dive depth. Technical cave training is required.
osm-n3149301713.access: Cave entry only practical when spring discharge is unusually low (as in 2007)
highlights: Deepest known freshwater cave system in the US

osm-n3167637595.name: Troy Spring
highlights: Civil War steamboat Madison scuttled in 1863
osm-n3167637595.summary: A 70-ft-deep spring on the Suwannee River whose main draw is the steamboat Madison, scuttled in 1863 to keep it from capture. Open for swimming, snorkeling and diving.

osm-n356542710.name: Edmonds Underwater Park
osm-n356542710.access: No diving within 100 yards of ferry landing; no night diving without permit
hazards: Steel dry dock interferes with compass
Long swims from shore
osm-n356542710.summary: A city-run shore-entry underwater park beside the Edmonds ferry dock, with a sunken dry dock, boats and reef structures linked by guide ropes. Popular with newer divers, though visibility varies and swims are long.

osm-n3582426705.name: Mango Bay
highlights: Schools of fusiliers and snapper in the shallows
Whiprays under big boulders
osm-n3582426705.summary: Sheltered, sandy-bottomed bay on Ko Tao with boulders and shallow reef, reached by boat. Mostly 2-15 m with light current, so it suits training dives and beginners.

osm-n408451459.name: Shaab Claudio
highlights: Shallow cave system with light shafts
osm-n408451459.summary: A shallow reef in the Fury Shoals with a spacious, partly open-roofed cave network, popular for sunbeams and photography. Maximum depth is about 16 m, though currents can be strong on the approach.

osm-n5760423321.name: Sebayor Kecil Dive Site
osm-n5760423321.depthNote: Catalog spelling is Sebayor; sources call the island and site Sebayur Kecil.
highlights: Bumphead parrotfish schools and turtles

osm-n5767096953.name: Cystal Rock Dive Site
highlights: Barracuda schools, grey and whitetip reef sharks
hazards: Strong current; reef hook recommended
osm-n5767096953.summary: A current-swept seamount pinnacle in northern Komodo National Park, known for clear water and abundant sharks and pelagics. Best for confident divers comfortable with drifts and hooks.

osm-n663869446.name: USS Oriskany
osm-n663869446.depthNote: Island top 84 ft, flight deck ~145 ft, seafloor 212 ft
highlights: Island structure within recreational depths
Hangar bay open to tech divers
hazards: Below 135 ft requires technical training
osm-n663869446.summary: A huge decommissioned aircraft carrier sunk upright off Pensacola as an artificial reef. Recreational divers visit the island superstructure while the flight deck and hangar bay below call for advanced or technical training.
sources: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission

osm-n663869447.name: USS Massachusetts
highlights: Turrets, cupolas and anchor chain
Goliath groupers and turtles
hazards: Strong surge and low visibility at wrong tide
osm-n663869447.summary: A pre-dreadnought battleship scuttled in very shallow water near Pensacola Pass. Its turrets sit close to the surface and attract a full reef community; timing the dive for slack high tide keeps surge and silt down.

osm-n663869451.name: San Pablo
highlights: Boilers, refrigeration coils and twisted steel
Dense toadfish population
osm-n663869451.summary: A WWII freighter destroyed in a secret 1944 weapons test, now a Florida Panhandle Shipwreck Trail dive off Pensacola. The scattered wreckage covers a wide stretch of sand, with boilers and plating that hold plenty of fish.

osm-n663869458.name: S.S. Inchulva / Delray Wreck
osm-n663869458.summary: The remains of a steamship wrecked in a 1903 hurricane lie just off Delray Beach's public beach in about 25 ft of water. The shallow depth and short distance from shore make it a popular first wreck for newer divers and snorkelers.

osm-n663869492.name: Bedfordshire (Wreck)
highlights: WWII British armed trawler lying in two sections
hazards: Unexploded depth charges near the stern
osm-n663869492.summary: A British anti-submarine trawler torpedoed off Cape Lookout in 1942, lying in about 105 ft in Gulf Stream water. The broken hull is a war grave, so divers look and do not penetrate.

osm-n663869494.name: U-701 (Wreck)
osm-n663869494.depthNote: Pin is ~3400 m deep; likely misplaced
hazards: Current swings from slight to very swift
Shifting sand changes what is exposed
osm-n663869494.summary: A WWII U-boat partly buried in sand about 20 miles off Cape Hatteras, where Gulf Stream and Labrador Current meet. Visibility and current vary widely, and the sand covers or exposes the hull year to year.

osm-n663869496.name: U-85 (Wreck)
highlights: Torpedo tubes with torpedoes still inside
Deck gun and conning tower
Sand tiger sharks
hazards: Visibility and temperature swing with shifting currents
osm-n663869496.summary: The first U-boat sunk off the US coast in WWII, lying on its side about 14 miles off Oregon Inlet. Battle damage, torpedo tubes and the conning tower are visible, but conditions change with the currents.

osm-n663869497.name: U-352 (Wreck)
highlights: Intact WWII U-boat
Amberjacks and great barracuda around the hull
osm-n663869497.summary: A German U-boat sunk in 1942, sitting largely intact in about 110 ft of Gulf Stream water off Morehead City. It draws baitfish and big predators; penetration is not permitted.

osm-n663869498.name: Indra (Wreck)
highlights: Abundant marine life; occasional sand tigers

osm-n663869499.name: Aeolus (Wreck)
highlights: Sand tiger sharks
Multi-level dive on a broken-up hull
osm-n663869499.summary: A 409 ft former cable ship sunk as a reef in 1988 and later broken into three sections by hurricanes, giving a multi-level wreck dive. Sand tigers often shelter on it.

osm-n663869517.name: Water Witch
highlights: One of the oldest intact commercial sailing ships
hazards: Zero visibility after heavy rain (Otter Creek runoff)
Surface and bottom currents
Fragile wreck; control buoyancy
osm-n663869517.summary: A remarkably intact lake sailing vessel resting about a quarter mile south of Diamond Island on Lake Champlain, within a Vermont underwater preserve. At about 90 ft with lights required, it suits very experienced divers.

osm-n663869518.name: Phoenix
osm-n663869518.depthNote: Bow 60 ft, stern 110 ft; buoy anchor pad about 50 ft
osm-n663869518.mooring: Preserve buoy; anchor pad about 50 ft down
highlights: Fire-charred framing and massive hull
hazards: Steep wreck angle can disorient divers
Lights needed; deep open-lake site needs planning
osm-n663869518.summary: A burned 19th-century paddle steamer lying on the north side of Colchester Shoal, protected as a Vermont underwater preserve. The hull slopes from roughly 60 ft at the bow to 110 ft at the stern; it is rated advanced and calls for lights and careful planning.

osm-n663869519.name: Burlington Bay Horse Ferry
osm-n663869519.access: Free, but divers must register annually
highlights: Only known surviving turntable horse ferry
Paddle wheels with iron hubs and oak spokes
hazards: Fragile paddle wheels; do not touch
Low visibility if bottom is stirred
osm-n663869519.summary: A 63-ft horse-powered ferry, the only known surviving turntable team-boat, lying at about 50 ft in Burlington Bay. A fragile intermediate-level preserve dive; hover and avoid touching the paddle wheels.

osm-n663869520.name: Champlain II
osm-n663869520.access: Free, but divers must register annually; shoreline is private
highlights: 163 ft of the 244 ft steamboat hull remains
Massive engine mounts on either side
hazards: Silty bottom, limited visibility
Zebra mussels cut hands; wear gloves
Unstable sternpost, overhanging sections
osm-n663869520.summary: A shallow Lake Champlain preserve wreck: the remaining 163 ft of an 1868 steamboat hull lies in 15-35 ft near the New York shore north of Westport. Easy beginner dive; keep off the silty bottom.

osm-n663869521.name: O.J. Walker
osm-n663869521.access: Free, but divers must register annually
highlights: Ship's wheel and aft cabin hatch cover
Masts, boom, anchors and rigging on site
hazards: Do not penetrate the wreck
Low visibility if bottom is stirred
osm-n663869521.summary: An 86-ft schooner-rigged canal boat lost in a storm in 1895, lying at about 65 ft off the Burlington breakwater. A state preserve dive for intermediate or experienced divers, with the wheel and rigging still on the wreck.

osm-n663869522.name: General Butler
osm-n663869522.access: Free, but divers must register annually
highlights: Remarkably intact 1862 canal schooner, upright
Windlass, cleats and dead-eyes in place
hazards: Extremely fragile rudder at the stern
Poor buoyancy control damages the wreck
osm-n663869522.summary: An upright 88-ft sailing canal boat from 1862 that struck the Burlington breakwater in a gale. At about 40 ft it is a beginner dive in a state preserve, with deck hatches and sailing hardware still in place.

osm-n663869532.name: Cedarville (Wreck)
osm-n663869532.mooring: Bow and stern mooring buoys, typically late May to mid-September
osm-n663869532.penetration: Penetration not advised without proper training, experience and equipment
highlights: Huge upside-down lake freighter
hazards: Large, deep, inverted wreck with variable visibility
osm-n663869532.summary: A big lake freighter lost in a 1965 collision east of the Mackinac Bridge, now lying inverted in the Straits of Mackinac Shipwreck Preserve from about 40 to 110 ft. Moorings make it reachable, but size, depth and poor visibility demand caution.

osm-n663869534.name: Panther (Wreck)
osm-n663869534.summary: A wooden grain steamer rammed in Whitefish Bay in 1916 and found in 1975, now resting at roughly 90 to 110 ft in the Whitefish Point Underwater Preserve on Lake Superior.

osm-n663869549.name: UB-81
osm-n663869549.reason: Designated controlled site under Protection of Military Remains Act 1986; diving prohibited

osm-n663869563.name: Vivian Quarry
osm-n663869563.access: Operator-run site; entry fee; check current opening status
highlights: Flooded buildings, boats, van and a submarine
osm-n663869563.summary: A flooded slate quarry section at Llanberis with a platform at 6 m and a floor around 18-20 m. Divers pass old mine buildings, rails and sunken boats; entry is through the on-site dive operator.

osm-n663869622.name: SMS König
highlights: Upturned hull opened up by salvage blasting
Casemate guns lying upside down on seabed
hazards: Blast debris scattered along the hull
osm-n663869622.summary: Upturned WWI German battleship east of Cava, scuttled in 1919 and heavily broken by salvage blasting. Less impressive than her sisters but the openings reveal internal structure; the hull top is around 20 m.

osm-n663869624.name: SMS Markgraf
osm-n663869624.access: Orkney Islands Council Harbours diving permit; scheduled monument
osm-n663869624.summary: Deepest of the three scuttled German battleships at Scapa Flow, lying upside down on its port side, with the hull rising to roughly 23 m above a seabed near 45 m. A demanding, deeper dive than its sisters.

osm-n663869630.name: SMS Cöln
osm-n663869630.access: Orkney Islands Council Harbours diving permit; scheduled monument
osm-n663869630.summary: German light cruiser scuttled in 1919 and never raised, resting on her starboard side in Scapa Flow. Her top is about 22 m and the seabed 36 m, and she is a straightforward wreck for competent sport divers.

osm-n663869632.name: SMS Kronprinz Wilhelm
osm-n663869632.access: Orkney Islands Council Harbours diving permit; scheduled monument, no removing artefacts
highlights: Half of the 12-inch guns still visible
Engine and boiler rooms explorable
osm-n663869632.summary: Upturned German battleship scuttled in 1919 in Scapa Flow, the shallowest of the big three. Its hull top is near 12-14 m and several main guns can be seen, making it the most approachable battleship dive.

osm-n663869681.name: Umbria
highlights: Holds still stacked with bombs and trucks
hazards: Munitions remain aboard the wreck
osm-n663869681.summary: A large Italian ship scuttled in 1940 near Wingate Reef, close to Port Sudan. It rests tilted on its port side with the top only a few metres down, still carrying its wartime cargo, and is regarded as one of the Red Sea's best wreck dives.

osm-n663869765.name: Abu Galawa Kebir
osm-n663869765.depthNote: Wreck 5-18 m; surrounding reef to about 35 m
osm-n663869765.summary: Small Chinese vessel sunk in 1943 on the Abu Galawa Kebir reef in the Fury Shoals. It lies shallow, roughly 5 to 18 m, and has long since grown into the reef, with the reef itself falling to about 35 m.

osm-n663869769.name: Hamada
highlights: Parts shallow enough to snorkel
Intact propeller
osm-n663869769.summary: A roughly 65 m cargo ship lying on its side on an inshore reef at Abu Ghosum south of Marsa Alam, in only about 14 m of water. Easy and photogenic, suitable for all experience levels.

osm-n663869779.name: Numidia
osm-n663869779.depthNote: Big Brother, bow near reef top, stern ~70-80 m
hazards: Strong current, risk of being swept off the reef
Prop lies beyond recreational depth
osm-n663869779.summary: A long steamship wreck on the Big Brother reef, reached only by liveaboard. The bow sits near 8 m while the hull falls past 80 m, so most divers see the upper sections in a current that can be fierce.

osm-n663869780.name: Aida
osm-n663869780.depthNote: Wreck at Big Brother; pin is Little Brother side area
hazards: Severe current exposure
osm-n663869780.summary: A small supply ship wrecked on the Brothers reef and now lying on a steep slope. It is a demanding, current-swept dive for experienced wreck divers, reachable only from liveaboards.

osm-n663869792.name: Shaab Sabrina
osm-n663869792.mooring: Boats moor on the southern reef side

osm-n663869809.name: Carnatic
osm-n663869809.penetration: Easy entry and exit through the open iron framework
highlights: Sea fans covering the skeletal ribs
hazards: Current can be strong and shift quickly
osm-n663869809.summary: A 19th-century iron steamship wreck on Abu Nuhas, resting on its port side with the bow far shallower than the stern. The open framework is easy to swim through and heavily covered in sea fans and coral.

osm-n663869810.name: Chrisoula K
osm-n663869810.penetration: Full penetration possible in certain areas for experienced wreck divers
highlights: Cargo of floor tiles still stacked in crates
hazards: Current can be strong and shift quickly
osm-n663869810.summary: An upright cargo freighter on Abu Nuhas whose bow almost reaches the surface and whose stern rests near 28 m. Its hold still contains stacked tiles and experienced wreck divers can enter parts of the interior.

osm-n663869811.name: Kimon M
osm-n663869811.penetration: Engineering department and holds are fairly easy to enter
highlights: Large groupers and schooling snappers
hazards: Current can be strong and shift quickly
osm-n663869811.summary: The deepest of the four Abu Nuhas wrecks, a freighter that slid off the reef to rest around 30 m. Divers can reach the engine spaces and holds, and groupers and snappers gather on the hull.

osm-n663869812.name: Giannis D
highlights: Glassfish clouds and trevally around the mast
Engine room, crew quarters and bridge to explore
hazards: Disorienting tilted interior
Current can be strong and shift quickly
osm-n663869812.summary: A large cargo ship lying on its side on Abu Nuhas reef, with the mast near the surface and the stern around 24 m. Experienced wreck divers can swim into the engine room and bridge, though the tilt is disorienting.

osm-n663869819.name: Dunraven
highlights: Inverted hull with swim-through by the boiler
Thousands of glassfish at the exit
osm-n663869819.summary: The Dunraven sank in 1876 on the Beacon Rock reef at the northwest edge of Ras Mohammed and now lies upside down in two sections, from about 15 m at the bow to 29-30 m at the stern, heavily encrusted with coral and glassfish.

osm-n663869830.name: Ras Umm Sid
osm-n663869830.depthNote: Pin id is Ras Umm Sid (Sharm); sources describe the Sharm site
highlights: Column of gorgonian fans from 14 to 28 m
Giant sea fan collections
hazards: Currents can be strong
osm-n663869830.summary: A fringing reef beneath the Ras Umm Sid lighthouse near Sharm el Sheikh, known for a band of large gorgonian sea fans along the wall and a coral garden on the plateau. Currents can pick up, so a drift suits it.

osm-n663869852.name: Kormoran
hazards: Dive only possible on very calm days
osm-n663869852.summary: A shallow cargo ship wreck lying in the Straits of Tiran since 1984, with its winch, engine and propeller all within about 12 m. Suitable for all levels but accessible only in very calm weather.

osm-n663869865.name: Ras Abu Galum
osm-n663869865.reason: Ras Abu Galum is a 400 sq km protectorate with several dive sites, not one site

osm-n663869869.name: Blue Hole
osm-n663869869.depthNote: Hole just over 100 m; Arch ceiling at 55 m
highlights: Saddle opening to the sea at about 6 m
Popular freediving venue
hazards: The Arch (ceiling 55 m) has killed many divers
Inward current through the Arch
osm-n663869869.summary: A circular sinkhole on the Gulf of Aqaba shore north of Dahab, just over 100 m deep, reached by walking in. Recreational divers keep to about 30 m on the Bells route; the Arch at 55 m is a notorious technical hazard.

osm-n663869872.name: Canyon
highlights: Open-topped canyon with glassfish and light shafts
Octopus, stonefish and scorpionfish
osm-n663869872.summary: A shore dive north of Dahab that crosses a shallow lagoon and coral garden to a deep open-topped fissure in the reef, filled with glassfish and lit by shafts of light. Intermediate level, roughly 5 to 30 m.

osm-n663869877.name: Cedar Pride
osm-n663869877.mooring: Boats tie up to a buoy about 200 m offshore
highlights: Overgrown crow's nest, much photographed
Good night dive site
osm-n663869877.summary: A Lebanese freighter deliberately sunk off Aqaba in 1985, now a coral-encrusted artificial reef lying on its port side. Its starboard side begins around 10 m, with gentle conditions that suit newer wreck divers.

osm-n6748047776.name: U-1105
osm-n6748047776.access: Maryland historic shipwreck preserve; no commercial charters operate there
hazards: Near-zero visibility and strong currents
osm-n6748047776.summary: A German Type VII submarine sunk in the Potomac after the war and now Maryland's first historic shipwreck preserve. It sits upright in deep, dark, current-swept water, so it is an advanced dive with a buoy on site in season.

osm-n7182771889.name: Wainilu
highlights: Macro critters on sand and rubble
hazards: Rare, highly venomous blue-ringed octopus

osm-n7669564569.name: Pendennis Shore Dive
highlights: Remains of two WWI U-boats
Reef with gullies and sand patches
hazards: Summer boat traffic; use a surface marker
osm-n7669564569.summary: Easy Falmouth shore dive, known as Silver Steps, entered down granite steps to a gully-cut reef about 10 m deep at high tide. Pieces of two scuttled U-boats lie to the north-east.

osm-n8559506183.name: Thomas reef
highlights: Plateau with a row of large gorgonian fans
Whitetip and leopard sharks on the ledge
hazards: Strong currents at the north and south ends
Thomas Canyon runs to 90 m; technical divers only
osm-n8559506183.summary: The smallest and most colourful of the four Tiran reefs, dived as a drift along a wall of gorgonians to a plateau near 25 m, with sharks resting on the ledge. Currents can be strong at either end.

osm-n8577535117.name: סטי"ל
osm-n8577535117.depthNote: Bridge 12 m, bow 18 m, stern 21 m, sand about 24-25 m
osm-n8577535117.access: Shore entry via ramp at Village Beach, Eilat
osm-n8577535117.penetration: Semi-penetration at bow and stern; some parts sealed
highlights: Bridge covered in soft purple coral
osm-n8577535117.summary: A decommissioned Israeli Navy missile boat sunk off Eilat in 1994 as a reef. It sits upright on sand a short swim from Village Beach, with a bridge near 12 m and a deck around 20 m, and parts of the interior can be explored.

osm-n8730688077.name: D1
osm-n8730688077.access: Protected wreck; divers may visit but nothing may be removed
osm-n8730688077.summary: Early Royal Navy submarine scuttled off Dartmouth in 1918 and rediscovered by technical divers, sitting upright and largely intact. It is now protected, so you can look but must leave everything in place.

osm-n9720994071.name: Shaab Rumi, Precontinent 2
highlights: Remains of Cousteau's undersea village
osm-n9720994071.summary: Remains of Cousteau's 1960s undersea habitat project on the Sha'ab Rumi reef off Sudan. Two structures were removed afterwards; the rest, including the submersible hangar and shark cages, is now a diveable relic.

osm-r11092421.name: Moucha Island
osm-r11092421.reason: A whole island with several dive sites around it, not one site

osm-r14353880.name: Brackett's Landing
osm-r14353880.summary: The beach access for Edmonds Underwater Park north of the ferry dock; divers swim out to a trail system of sunken vessels and reefs. Suited to novices, with variable visibility and lengthy swims.

osm-r20325186.name: HMS Port Napier
osm-r20325186.penetration: Possible through cut openings; take a twinset
highlights: Bow guns and kelp-covered port side
Light through cut openings in the hull
hazards: Shallow wreckage can hole a boat
Sharp metal at hull openings
osm-r20325186.summary: A minelayer lying on her starboard side in Loch Alsh off Skye, partly drying at low water. Wide range of dives from easy to penetration, reached by local charter boat from Kyle of Lochalsh or Kyleakin.

osm-w132766337.name: Dosthill Quarry
highlights: Training platforms at several depths
Plane, cars and vans on the bottom
hazards: Sudden drop-off to 24 m; needs good buoyancy
osm-w132766337.summary: A Staffordshire inland quarry with easy walk-in access, shallow training platforms and a steep drop to roughly 24-26 m. Sunken vehicles, a plane and trees add interest, and pike and sturgeon live there.

osm-w141329817.name: Eccleston Delph
highlights: Training platforms at 3-9 m
Rope lines linking underwater features
osm-w141329817.summary: A flooded Lancashire stone quarry used for training and fun diving, with platforms between 3 and 9 m, rope trails linking sunken features and a floor around 20 m. Visibility is typically 3-10 m.

osm-w23185891.name: Woodhouse Reef
osm-w23185891.mooring: No fixed moorings; drift south to north
highlights: Wall running from the surface down
Giant morays, groupers, barracuda and jacks
hazards: "Washing Machine" currents between Woodhouse and Jackson
osm-w23185891.summary: The longest reef in the Straits of Tiran, a wall dropping from the surface to about 30 m or more, dived as a south-to-north drift with a canyon midway. Currents build toward the north end where it meets Jackson Reef.

osm-w24920367.name: Stoney Cove
highlights: Stanegarth tug, bus, Viscount cockpit, galleon
hazards: Deep silt can drop visibility to zero
osm-w24920367.summary: A flooded inland quarry with terraced zones from about 7 m for beginners to 36 m for experts, scattered with sunken vehicles, aircraft parts and the Stanegarth tug. Silt at depth can kill visibility.

osm-w35332224.name: Dutch Springs
highlights: Sunken bus, fire engine, planes and boats
osm-w35332224.summary: A flooded Pennsylvania limestone quarry used for training and fun diving, with a school bus, fire engine, aircraft and boats placed between 20 and 100 ft. Visibility and temperature vary with the season.

osm-w643470454.name: Blue Water Park
highlights: Sunken sailboat, cars, school bus, fire trucks

osm-w952659147.name: S.S. Sapona
osm-w952659147.depthNote: Pin is in the Bahamas (Bimini), not the United States
highlights: Concrete ship partly above water with swim-throughs
osm-w952659147.summary: A WWI-era concrete freighter aground in shallow water off South Bimini, Bahamas (not the US). Holes from WWII bombing practice let light into swim-throughs, making it easy for snorkelers and new divers.

x-curated-589.name: Devil's Lake
x-curated-589.access: Surface flag required; no surface air pump or generator
highlights: Boulders, fallen trees and abundant fish
x-curated-589.summary: A clear inland lake in a Wisconsin state park, dived from the northeast shore near the far parking lot. Depth tops out around 45 ft, with boulders, sunken trees and plenty of fish, and no motorboats.

x-curated-590.name: Lake Wazee
x-curated-590.access: Dive and parking fees payable before entering the lake
highlights: Remains of mining roadways visible underwater
Underwater training platforms and fish cribs
hazards: Depth to about 355 ft
x-curated-590.summary: A flooded taconite pit near Black River Falls, Wisconsin, with clear water and a maximum depth around 350 ft. A county park offers beach entry, training platforms and old mining remnants, with dives for beginners to advanced.

x-curated-594.name: Bonne Terre Mine
x-curated-594.access: Guided dives only, groups of nine with two guides
x-curated-594.summary: A flooded former lead mine in Missouri, run as a guided dive resort with stadium-style lighting. Still, cool water and very long visibility let groups tour pillars, mining equipment and a flooded shaft.

x-curated-596.name: Roubidoux Spring
x-curated-596.depthNote: Cave dive; depth reached inside cave

x-curated-608.name: Lake Tahoe — Sand Harbor
x-curated-608.access: In summer diving is limited to Divers Cove at Sand Harbor State Park
x-curated-608.summary: Shore dive from Sand Harbor State Park on Lake Tahoe's Nevada side, with clear water and granite boulders. In summer only the small Divers Cove is open, and the cove is also a common training site.

x-curated-616.name: Lake Jocassee
x-curated-616.depthNote: Devils Fork dive sites 30-70 ft; lake itself deeper

x-curated-618.name: Peacock Springs
x-curated-618.depthNote: Cave-system maximum, not a normal open-water dive depth. Technical cave training is required.
x-curated-618.access: State park; certification card displayed on dashboard; cavern/cave cert needed in cave systems; no scooters
highlights: Over 38,000 ft of mapped passages
hazards: Overhead cave passages require cave certification
x-curated-618.summary: A Suwannee County state park holding one of the longest underwater cave networks in the continental U.S. Divers walk in from the car park, must show certification, and need cavern or cave training for most of the systems; scooters are banned.

x-notable-1002.name: HMS Sealion
x-notable-1002.reason: Wreck is in the Firth of Clyde off Pladda (~62 m), not at this North Sea pin

x-notable-1003.name: HMS Amphion
x-notable-1003.access: Protected military wreck; MoD permission needed to dive
x-notable-1003.summary: The first British warship lost in the First World War, a cruiser mined in 1914, sits upright but split in two around 37 m down about 40 miles off Harwich. Visits need Ministry of Defence permission, and visibility has been around 5 m.

x-notable-1009.name: SMS Nürnberg
x-notable-1009.reason: Beached, not sunk here; sunk as a target in 1922

x-notable-1012.name: RMS Oceanic
hazards: Dive only at slack water in calm seas
Swells and currents sweep the reef
x-notable-1012.summary: Wartime liner broken up on the Shaalds reef east of Foula, now scattered wreckage across a wide area, mostly shallow with some parts to about 20 m. Exposed site that can only be dived around slack water in calm seas.

x-notable-1020.name: Hollandia
hazards: Swell and strong tidal currents
x-notable-1020.summary: Dutch East India Company ship lost in 1743 on Gunner Rock off Annet in the Isles of Scilly. The scattered remains lie around 28 m and are exposed to swell and strong tidal streams.
sources: Cultural Heritage Agency of the Netherlands (MaSS)

x-notable-1026.name: USS Chub
x-notable-1026.reason: Not wrecked here: transferred to Turkey in 1948, later scrapped

x-notable-1033.name: HMS E49
x-notable-1033.access: Registered war grave; do not remove items (divers have been convicted)
x-notable-1033.summary: British E-class submarine mined in 1917 and lost with all hands in Balta Sound, Unst. She lies on sand around 29-32 m with the conning tower broken off; a war grave, so look but do not touch.

x-notable-1040.name: HMS Medway
x-notable-1040.reason: HMS Medway sank in the Mediterranean off Port Said (about 32.05N 30.92E); this pin is inland in the Nile Delta, and Egypt-labelled Red Sea/fresh water does not

x-notable-1042.name: HMS B2
highlights: Conning tower with hatch open
x-notable-1042.summary: A small Edwardian B-class submarine lost in 1912 and lying on sand and chalk northeast of Dover at around 25-33 m. The hull stands about 5 m high with the conning tower intact.
sources: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record

x-notable-1044.name: USS Stockton
hazards: Wreck mostly buried; structures stand 3-4 m off seabed
x-notable-1044.summary: A broken-up former US destroyer (later HMS Ludlow) used as a rocket target, lying off Yellowcraigs beach in about 6 m. Much is buried in sand in two sections, with remains breaking the surface at low tide.

x-notable-1048.name: HMS Argyll
x-notable-1048.summary: Scattered remains of a cruiser that ran onto the Bell Rock reef in 1915, lying in about 6 m just west of the lighthouse. Her guns and propellers were salvaged, but she is still regarded as diveable.

x-notable-1049.name: HMS Empress of India
hazards: Deep: beyond recreational limits
x-notable-1049.summary: A pre-dreadnought battleship sunk as a gunnery target in 1913; she lies capsized on sand in the middle of Lyme Bay at around 42 m, partly stripped by salvors.

x-notable-1050.name: HMS King Edward VII
x-notable-1050.depthNote: Least depth 94 m in 108 m general depth (1984 survey)
x-notable-1050.summary: Pre-dreadnought battleship lost to a German-laid mine in January 1916 and now a large wreck off the north coast, surveyed by side-scan sonar in 1984. At roughly 100 m it is a deep technical dive.

x-notable-1052.name: HMS Glatton
x-notable-1052.reason: Wreck moved within Dover harbour and buried by landfill under the car ferry terminal

x-notable-1053.name: HMS Campania
x-notable-1053.depthNote: Seabed 22-25 m; hull stands up to ~12 m proud
x-notable-1053.access: Historic Marine Protected Area: responsible diving encouraged, no artefact recovery, file a visit report with HES
x-notable-1053.summary: The remains of a Cunard liner turned seaplane carrier lie off Burntisland in the Firth of Forth, in roughly 22-25 m. A protected site, it is still a big upstanding iron hull that divers may visit under HES guidelines.

x-notable-1056.name: HMS A10
x-notable-1056.reason: Sank alongside at Ardrossan in 1917, raised and scrapped in 1919

x-notable-1057.name: HMS H41
x-notable-1057.reason: Sunk at Blyth in 1919 but raised and sold in 1920

x-notable-1058.name: HMS Cobra
x-notable-1058.reason: Designated a Controlled Site; cannot be dived without written MoD permission

x-notable-1063.name: Atago Maru
highlights: Hull covered with corals
x-notable-1063.summary: WWII Japanese ship sitting upright in about 14 m roughly 1.6 km off Miri, Sarawak, where it was bombed at anchor in 1944. Coral-encrusted and a popular local wreck dive; visibility can be challenging.

x-notable-1072.name: HMS Lynx
x-notable-1072.summary: A WWI destroyer mined in the Moray Firth in 1915, now well broken on a mud and sand seabed at about 57 m. Found by survey in 1991 and first dived in 2000; a technical-level dive.

x-notable-1074.name: HMS Wivern
x-notable-1074.reason: Destroyer sold for scrapping in 1947, not a wreck

x-notable-1081.name: U-1206
x-notable-1081.depthNote: Sources give 70 m (1970s survey) and 86 m (diver-identified)
highlights: Remarkably intact U-boat with open torpedo tubes

x-notable-1083.name: Great Basses wreck
x-notable-1083.access: Site is access-restricted; calm seas needed to reach the wreck
x-notable-1083.summary: Early 18th-century Mughal-era wreck wedged in a narrow trench between two reefs near the Great Basses lighthouse, about 12 km off Sri Lanka's south coast. Shallow, but reaching it needs exceptionally calm seas and the site is access-restricted.
sources: Sri Lanka National Shipwreck Database (Central Cultural Fund)

x-notable-1088.name: HMS Ariadne
highlights: Dispersed WW1 wreck, under 2 m tall
x-notable-1088.summary: A First World War cruiser-turned-minelayer torpedoed off Beachy Head and now scattered widely across the seabed. Eastbourne operators run it as a drift dive for experienced divers rather than a wreck to explore.

x-notable-1092.name: HMS Assurance
x-notable-1092.access: Protected wreck site licensed to the Maritime Archaeology Trust
highlights: Cannon and carronades strewn on the site
hazards: Highly dynamic seabed; dive on slack water
x-notable-1092.summary: A frigate lost at the Needles in the 18th century, now mixed with the remains of HMS Pomone on one protected wreck site. Divers find artefacts among chalk gullies, with little of the ship itself surviving.

x-notable-1103.name: HMS Hampshire
x-notable-1103.reason: Controlled site under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986; no diving without MoD licence

x-notable-1104.name: HMS Repulse
x-notable-1104.reason: HMS Repulse (1916) lies off Malaya; no wreck at this Scottish inland pin

x-notable-1110.name: HMS Seahorse
x-notable-1110.reason: Lost off Heligoland (54°19'N 7°30'E) in 1940 and never found; catalogue pin is in the central North Sea

x-notable-1114.name: HMS Iolaire
x-notable-1114.access: Protected war grave since Sept 2019; do not remove items
hazards: Badly broken up, scattered wreckage
x-notable-1114.summary: A badly broken-up WWI naval yacht lost on the Beasts of Holm at the entrance to Stornoway harbour, lying in roughly 11 m. It is a protected war grave, so look but do not touch.
sources: Comhairle nan Eilean Siar Historic Environment Record

x-notable-1120.name: HMS Stoic
x-notable-1120.reason: Submarine was sold and broken up at Dalmuir in 1950; no wreck exists

x-notable-1121.name: HMS Sirdar
x-notable-1121.reason: Not a wreck: sold and broken up for scrap in 1965

x-notable-1137.name: HMS Strongbow
x-notable-1137.reason: Submarine was scrapped at Preston in 1946; no wreck exists

x-notable-1141.name: HMS Formidable
x-notable-1141.summary: Pre-dreadnought battleship sunk by U-boat torpedoes on New Year's Day 1915 and now lying around 60 m down in the Channel. A deep wreck aimed at experienced technical divers.

x-notable-1149.name: HMHS Rewa
hazards: Strong currents and heavy silt
Wreck broken up by depth charging
x-notable-1149.summary: A torpedoed WWI hospital ship lying upright in about 60 m off north Devon and Cornwall. Currents and silt plus a collapsed, depth-charged hull make it a demanding site reserved for experienced technical divers.

x-notable-1158.name: IMO 6611461
x-notable-1158.mooring: Mooring line runs between the wreck and the dive boat
highlights: Rusting 385 ft ferry wreck grounded on the reef
Fish sheltering under and around the hull
hazards: Sharp rusty edges
Wreck may collapse suddenly
x-notable-1158.summary: The former cross-Channel ferry Free Enterprise III, later Al Fahad, ran aground on the Jeddah coast in 2004 and is now a boat-accessed wreck dive. Divers follow the mooring line past a corroding hull busy with reef fish.

x-notable-1168.name: SMS V46
x-notable-1168.reason: Beached, not sunk; broken up in 1924

x-notable-1184.name: USS Conestoga
highlights: Wolf eels, lingcod and rockfish
x-notable-1184.summary: A WWI-era Navy tug lost in 1921 and found in 2015 off the Farallon Islands, in deep water inside Greater Farallones sanctuary. It was documented by ROV and is largely intact, coated in plume anemones.
sources: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries

x-notable-1187.name: USS S-24
x-notable-1187.summary: An American S-class submarine lent to the Royal Navy and scuttled off Portland in 1947 as an asdic target. She sits upright and largely intact, with the deck at about 38 m and the seabed near 44 m.

x-notable-1190.name: USS Tarpon
highlights: Intact WWII submarine, upright
Sand tiger sharks
x-notable-1190.summary: A WWII submarine that sank under tow in 1957 and now lies upright in 135 ft off Cape Hatteras, covered in algae, anemones and corals. Sand tigers are frequent visitors.

x-notable-1192.name: United States lightship LV-117
hazards: Entangled in fishing nets
Unpredictable currents up to 3 knots
x-notable-1192.summary: A steel lightship rammed and sunk by the liner Olympic in 1934, lying on its side far offshore south of Nantucket. A deep, demanding wreck that is remarkably intact but tangled in nets.

x-notable-1197.name: BRP Sierra Madre
x-notable-1197.reason: Commissioned Philippine Navy vessel grounded at Second Thomas Shoal, manned by marines

x-notable-1201.name: MV Captayannis
hazards: Murky, silty water on a muddy seabed
Deck plates rusting through, holes opening up
x-notable-1201.summary: A sugar freighter that grounded on a sandbank in the middle of the Clyde between Greenock and Helensburgh, still partly above water at every tide. Below, the hull sits in murky, silty water around 9 m and is deteriorating.

x-notable-1203.name: SMS G102
x-notable-1203.reason: Beached, not sunk here; sunk as a target in 1921

x-notable-1206.name: HMS Labuan
x-notable-1206.reason: Frigate sold and scrapped in 1957, not a wreck

x-notable-1207.name: HMS Papua
x-notable-1207.reason: Ship survived the war and sank in the Gulf of Suez in 1953; no wreck off Rathlin

x-notable-1211.name: HMS Blackwater
highlights: Wreck stands about 8 m off the seabed
x-notable-1211.summary: A destroyer sunk in a 1909 collision off Dungeness, almost cut in two. Her remains rise about 8 m from a seabed at roughly 28 m, making a moderately deep boat dive.

x-notable-1212.name: HMS Erne
x-notable-1212.reason: Driven ashore on sand at Rattray Head in 1915 and broken up in place; only remains exposed at low water

x-notable-1215.name: HMCS Trentonian
x-notable-1215.summary: Canadian Flower-class corvette torpedoed off Falmouth in February 1945; the 63 m hull lies at about 65 m, a technical-diver wreck.

x-notable-1218.name: HMS K17
x-notable-1218.access: Protected place under the Protection of Military Remains Act 1986 (war grave)

x-notable-1221.name: SM UB-116
highlights: Conning tower, ballast tanks and deck gun remain
hazards: Wreck very broken up after torpedo clearance
x-notable-1221.summary: The last U-boat sunk in WWI, destroyed by a mine in Hoxa Sound in 1918, raised, then lost again at the mouth of Pan Hope off Flotta. Small, shallow for Scapa and badly broken, so an easy second dive.

x-notable-1222.name: HMS Venetia
x-notable-1222.depthNote: Least depth 43.7 ft, general 48 ft, scour 52 ft (1973 survey, LAT)
hazards: Wreck dispersed and hard to find
x-notable-1222.summary: A First World War-era destroyer mined in the Thames Estuary in December 1940. Hydrographic surveys describe broken-up wreckage in roughly 14-15 m, with a scour beside it, and it has been hard to locate.
sources: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record

x-notable-1228.name: SS City of Chester
hazards: Strong Golden Gate currents, cold water
x-notable-1228.summary: An 1888 passenger steamer lying upright in mud off the Golden Gate in over 200 ft. Cold water and strong currents make it a very experienced-diver-only site; the hull is largely rotted away.

x-notable-1231.name: SS Pendleton
x-notable-1231.access: Exempted wreck site in Massachusetts; diving allowed but removing or disturbing wreckage is unlawful
hazards: Jagged metal left over from the blast
Rough water; suited to experienced divers
x-notable-1231.summary: Shallow, broken remains of a wrecked ship's stern section off Monomoy near Chatham, Cape Cod. Rough water and sharp wreckage make it a dive for experienced divers; it may be dived but not disturbed.

x-notable-1237.name: Beeswax wreck
x-notable-1237.reason: Only scattered remnants found; main hull of the galleon never located

x-notable-1240.name: HMS Pheasant
x-notable-1240.access: Protected under the Military Remains Act 1986
hazards: Wreck heavily broken from bow to bridge
x-notable-1240.summary: M-class destroyer lost with all hands to a mine west of Hoy in March 1917. She lies on her side in about 82 m, broken forward of the bridge, so it is a deep technical dive on a protected war wreck.

x-notable-1244.name: HMS Jason
x-notable-1244.access: War grave; exact position not published
x-notable-1244.summary: A WWI minesweeper that struck a mine between Mull and Coll in 1917 and lies broken in about 93 m, relocated by divers in 2022. A trimix-level war grave dive.

x-notable-1245.name: Blessing of Burntisland
x-notable-1245.reason: The ship has never been positively found or identified

x-notable-1254.name: HMS Sword Dance (possibly)
x-notable-1254.depthNote: Echo-sounder survey; identification as Sword Dance unconfirmed

x-notable-1260.name: USS LSM-333
x-notable-1260.depthNote: Top of wreck about 10 m, seabed 30 m
x-notable-1260.penetration: Swim-throughs of the upper deck down into the engine room
x-notable-1260.summary: Ex-US landing ship (HTMS Kut) sunk as an artificial reef near Ko Sak in Pattaya Bay, upright in about 30 m with the top near 10 m. Advanced-level dive with deck swim-throughs into the engine room.

x-notable-1266.name: Mortar Wreck
x-notable-1266.access: Protected wreck; dive only under a Historic England licence
highlights: 13th-century hull under a mound of Purbeck stone
x-notable-1266.summary: A medieval cargo vessel in Poole Bay carrying quarried Purbeck stone, designated a protected wreck in 2022. The site is a small mound of stone over the hull remains and can only be dived with a licence.

x-notable-1279.name: HMS G11
hazards: Large air cylinders litter the site

x-notable-1283.name: HMS Hollyhock
highlights: Bow section relatively well preserved
Exposed boilers; stern in debris field
hazards: Currents can be very strong
x-notable-1283.summary: WWII corvette lying 30-42 m on the seabed near a slope, around 15 km off Oluvil on the east coast. The bow is the best-preserved part while the stern is scattered; currents can run hard.
sources: Sri Lanka National Shipwreck Database (Central Cultural Fund)

x-notable-1287.name: HMS K13
x-notable-1287.reason: Raised in 1917, recommissioned as K22 and later scrapped; no wreck on the Gareloch seabed

x-notable-1288.name: HMS Laforey
x-notable-1288.summary: First World War destroyer lost to a mine in 1917 that split her in two. The remains are dived from Sussex boats out of Shoreham, though no depth could be confirmed.

x-notable-1291.name: HMS Loch Fada
x-notable-1291.reason: Frigate scrapped in 1970, not a wreck

x-notable-1292.name: HMS Looe
highlights: Iron ballast stack and scattered artifacts of 1744 frigate
x-notable-1292.summary: The remains of an 18th-century British frigate lost in 1744 on the eastern edge of Looe Key reef off Big Pine Key. Shallow, clear water and the stacked iron ballast make it an easy historic wreck dive.

x-notable-1300.name: HMS Success
x-notable-1300.reason: Salvaged after grounding off Kingsbarns; little remains, only part of the keel in the shallows

x-notable-1302.name: HMS Tenedos
x-notable-1302.reason: Sunk in Colombo harbour 1942; wreck removed by a salvage vessel in 1944

x-notable-1307.name: HMS Whiting
x-notable-1307.reason: Wreck is off Padstow (Doom Bar), Cornwall, not the Firth of Forth; sand covers the site and it has not been located

x-notable-1312.name: HMT Amethyst
x-notable-1312.depthNote: Least depth 15.8 m, general seabed 18.7 m (LAT soundings); scour to 22.4 m
highlights: Large wreck, easy to locate
x-notable-1312.summary: An anti-submarine trawler sunk by a mine in 1940 in the Barrow Deep, Thames Estuary. Survey records show a sizeable, easily found wreck with a scour hole, its shallowest part around 16 m below chart datum.
sources: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record

x-notable-1315.name: HMT Warwick Deeping
x-notable-1315.depthNote: Deckhouse roof about 30 m, seabed 34-37 m
highlights: Intact trawler with 4.7in gun at the bow
Iron four-blade propeller exposed by scour
hazards: Strong tide; slack water short and essential
Net draped over the forward wreck; scour under stern
x-notable-1315.summary: A small armed trawler lost in 1940, sitting upright and largely intact on gravel in 34 to 37 m south of the Isle of Wight. It lies along the tide, so a short slack-water window and careful shotting matter.

x-notable-1316.name: HMY Mary
x-notable-1316.depthNote: Gullies hold remains from 5 m to 25 m
x-notable-1316.access: Protected wreck (Protection of Wrecks Act 1973); diving needs a Welsh Government licence
hazards: Exposed site with strong currents
x-notable-1316.summary: A royal yacht lost in 1675 at the Skerries off Anglesey, now a heavily concreted ballast mound at the foot of a cliff with finds in rocky gullies. It is a designated historic wreck and exposed to wind and tide.

x-notable-776.name: SMS Grosser Kurfürst
x-notable-776.access: Scheduled monument; recreational diving allowed, no salvage or removal
x-notable-776.summary: A large 1870s German ironclad that sank in a collision off Folkestone and now lies capsized and partly collapsed. Scheduled in 2020, it can still be visited by recreational divers who leave everything in place.

x-notable-779.name: Brother Jonathan
x-notable-779.depthNote: Reported 260 to 275 ft depending on source
hazards: Underwater currents and darkness
Murky water at about 260-275 ft
x-notable-779.summary: Historic steamer lost on the rocks off Point St. George near Crescent City in 1865 and found by minisub in 1993. It lies roughly 260-275 ft down in murky, current-swept water, well beyond recreational limits.

x-notable-781.name: Earl of Abergavenny
highlights: About 140 ft of keel exposed
1805 East Indiaman wreck
x-notable-781.summary: The remains of an East Indiaman lost on the Shambles reef in 1805 and later blasted as a navigation hazard. Today it is a low, flattened site off Weymouth, with the keel exposed in roughly 17 m of water, reached by boat.

x-notable-785.name: SS City of Rio de Janeiro
hazards: Strong currents and great depth off the Golden Gate
x-notable-785.summary: The 1901 passenger steamer lies deep off the Golden Gate, found again by NOAA sonar surveys. Depth and strong currents put it beyond ordinary recreational diving; it is a site for technical or professional teams.
sources: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries

x-notable-787.name: U-85
highlights: Torpedo tubes with torpedoes still inside
Deck gun and conning tower
Sand tiger sharks
hazards: Visibility and temperature swing with shifting currents
x-notable-787.summary: The first U-boat sunk off the US coast in WWII, lying on its side about 14 miles off Oregon Inlet. Battle damage, torpedo tubes and the conning tower are visible, but conditions change with the currents.

x-notable-788.name: Half Moon
x-notable-788.access: Florida Underwater Archaeological Preserve; open year round, free of charge
highlights: Damselfish, sergeant majors, spiny lobster, angelfish
x-notable-788.summary: The 1930 wreck of a former racing yacht sits on a shoal off Key Biscayne in only 8-10 ft of water, with just a few feet over the hull. A free state archaeological preserve with mooring balls, it suits snorkelers and relaxed shallow dives.

x-notable-792.name: SM U-8
x-notable-792.access: Protected wreck (Protection of Wrecks Act 1973); licence needed
hazards: Large net hanging off the stern
Busy Dover shipping separation zone
x-notable-792.summary: A First World War German U-boat lying upright in the Dover Strait, with its decks around 32 m and the sand scour deeper still. It is a legally protected wreck, so visits are by licence, and fishing net and line snag the stern.
sources: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record

x-notable-793.name: HMS Association
x-notable-793.access: Protected wreck: licence under the Protection of Wrecks Act; licensed Scilly charter boats only
highlights: Iron cannon, anchors and round shot on the seabed
hazards: Deep rock gullies and large boulders
Many guns trapped beneath boulders
x-notable-793.summary: Flagship wreck of the 1707 Scilly disaster, now a licensed protected site around the Gilstone Ledges. Divers move through rocky gullies on a seabed that falls away from the reef, finding scattered iron guns and anchors.
sources: Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Maritime Archaeology Society (Virtual Dive Trails)

x-notable-794.name: HMS Invincible
x-notable-794.access: Protected wreck monitored by a licensee
highlights: Large hull timbers protrude from the seabed
hazards: Dirty water and tidal flow in the Solent
x-notable-794.summary: An 18th century warship lying in the eastern Solent, mostly buried in sand but with large hull timbers showing. It is a protected wreck under licensed archaeological investigation, in shallow water with variable visibility.
sources: University of Southampton Centre for Maritime Archaeology

x-notable-798.name: Urca de Lima
x-notable-798.access: Underwater archaeological preserve; free, open year round; no souvenir collecting
highlights: Sea urchins, flounder, wrasse and blue tang
x-notable-798.summary: Florida's first underwater archaeological preserve: the scattered remains of a 1715 Spanish treasure fleet ship lie 200 yards off Fort Pierce in 10-15 ft of water. Shallow and free to visit, it is a good snorkel or easy dive.

x-notable-802.name: HMT Bedfordshire
highlights: WWII British armed trawler lying in two sections
hazards: Unexploded depth charges near the stern
x-notable-802.summary: A British anti-submarine trawler torpedoed off Cape Lookout in 1942, lying in about 105 ft in Gulf Stream water. The broken hull is a war grave, so divers look and do not penetrate.

x-notable-807.name: HMS H5
x-notable-807.reason: Controlled site under the Protection of Military Remains Act; diving prohibited without MoD licence

x-notable-808.name: HMS H47
x-notable-808.reason: Wreck not confirmed at the recorded position
sources: Coflein (Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales)

x-notable-811.name: HMS Resistance
x-notable-811.reason: Foundered in 1899 but raised and broken up ashore at Garston

x-notable-812.name: HMS Whirlwind
x-notable-812.depthNote: Coflein 31 m; Divernet tour 35-45 m range, 36 m on the seabed
highlights: Cold War frigate with a relatively intact hull
hazards: Dive only at slack water
Easy to run into decompression on one dive
x-notable-812.summary: A Cold War frigate that foundered in Cardigan Bay in 1974 while being used as a trial target. It lies on its port side in about 31-36 m, best done on slack water by experienced divers, with a largely intact hull.
sources: Coflein (Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales)

x-notable-813.name: Cattewater Wreck
x-notable-813.access: Protected wreck; licence required; hull is buried under sediment
x-notable-813.summary: Early Tudor merchant ship in Plymouth's Cattewater, the first wreck protected under the 1973 Act. The timbers lie under silt and only a scaffold pole shows, so there is little to see and a licence is needed.

x-notable-814.name: HMS Anne
x-notable-814.reason: Beached wreck buried in Pett Level foreshore, visited on foot at very low tide

x-notable-815.name: HMS Colossus
x-notable-815.access: Protected wreck: licence needed to dive; dive trail for licensed visitors
highlights: Numbered dive trail past cannon and hull timbers
x-notable-815.summary: Shallow Napoleonic-era warship wreck off Samson in the Isles of Scilly with a marked dive trail. It lies about 10 m down and visiting divers need a licence as a protected wreck.

x-notable-816.name: HMS London
x-notable-816.access: Protected wreck (Protection of Wrecks Act 1973); diving only under licence, by the licensee's volunteer team
hazards: Very poor visibility, around 50 cm on a good day
x-notable-816.summary: The 1665 warship London lies in two pieces in the Thames Estuary off Southend. It is a legally protected wreck worked by a licensed volunteer dive team in very murky water, so it is not a casual recreational dive.

x-notable-817.name: HMS Northumberland
x-notable-817.access: Protected wreck site; diving by licence only
x-notable-817.summary: A 70-gun ship of the line lost on the Goodwin Sands in the 1703 storm, now a low mound with much of the structure buried in sand. It is a protected wreck monitored by a licensee.

x-notable-819.name: HMS Stirling Castle
hazards: Wreck repeatedly buried and uncovered by sand
x-notable-819.summary: A 1703 warship on the Goodwin Sands in roughly 12-15 m, found by recreational divers in 1979. Sand covers and re-exposes it, and it is a protected wreck.
sources: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record

x-notable-824.name: South Australian
x-notable-824.access: Scheduled monument; divers may visit but not disturb
highlights: Large stack of iron rails rising about 4 m
x-notable-824.summary: A clipper carrying a cargo of iron rails, lying near 42 m northeast of Lundy. Scheduled as a monument in 2019, it remains open to deep, experienced leisure divers who leave it undisturbed.

x-notable-825.name: SS Aleutian
hazards: Depth, current and low visibility
x-notable-825.summary: A 360-ft Alaska Steamship liner that struck a pinnacle in Uyak Bay, Kodiak Island, in 1929 and now sits upright and remarkably intact on the seabed at about 220 ft. Only experienced deep-wreck divers can reach it.

x-notable-826.name: SS Regina
sources: Florida Dept. of State / FPAN Museums in the Sea

x-notable-828.name: SS Tarpon
x-notable-828.access: Florida Underwater Archaeological Preserve; open year round, free of charge
hazards: Visibility can turn murky after rain
x-notable-828.summary: The remains of a 160-foot Gulf coast steamer lie about eight nautical miles off Panama City at roughly 90 to 95 feet. It is a state underwater archaeological preserve that has become a reef for corals, grunts and amberjacks.

x-notable-830.name: USCS Robert J. Walker
x-notable-830.summary: An iron-hulled survey steamer lost in a collision in 1860 and lying about ten miles off the New Jersey coast. A long-time regular destination for wreck divers, its identity was confirmed by NOAA in 2013.

x-notable-831.name: Vamar Shipwreck Site
sources: Florida Dept. of State / FPAN Museums in the Sea

x-notable-832.name: USS New Hampshire
highlights: Copper spikes and small artifacts in the sand
x-notable-832.summary: Broken-up remains of a burned 19th-century ship of the line off Graves Island, Manchester-by-the-Sea, in about 30 ft of water. The hull is mostly sand-covered; copper spikes can still be found.

x-notable-838.name: Rothsay Castle
x-notable-838.reason: Coflein: wreck remains not confirmed at this location

x-notable-839.name: HMS Cleveland
x-notable-839.reason: Wrecked on Rhossili beach in 1957 and broken up and cleared on the beach
sources: Coflein (Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales)

x-notable-840.name: Hirano Maru
x-notable-840.reason: Coflein holds only a placeholder Bristol Channel location; wreck position unknown

x-notable-841.name: HMS Nimrod
x-notable-841.reason: Grounded at Holyhead in 1827 but sold and returned to service, so no wreck remains

x-notable-842.name: Rooswijk
x-notable-842.access: Protected wreck; permit required to visit
x-notable-842.summary: An 18th-century Dutch East Indiaman on the Goodwin Sands in about 24 m of water. A protected wreck, it can only be visited with a permit and diving qualification.
sources: Cultural Heritage Agency of the Netherlands

x-notable-843.name: SM UC-70
x-notable-843.access: Protected wreck (Protection of Wrecks Act 1973, designated 2017); diving only under licence
highlights: Mine-laying tubes, 88mm gun and conning tower remains
hazards: Poor visibility, especially at low-water slack
x-notable-843.summary: A WWI German minelaying submarine lying upright on the seabed a few miles off Whitby. It is a protected site; divers see mine tubes, deck gun and conning tower remains, best at high-water slack.

x-notable-845.name: Swash Channel Wreck
x-notable-845.summary: The partly buried hull of an early 17th century sailing ship on the edge of the Swash Channel at Poole Harbour entrance. It lies in 6 to 9 m and is a designated protected wreck, so access is controlled.

x-notable-846.name: Wheel Wreck
x-notable-846.access: Protected wreck: licence under the Protection of Wrecks Act; licensed Scilly charter boats only
highlights: Stack of iron wheels, cogs and pipes
x-notable-846.summary: Wreck south of Little Ganinick whose cargo of iron wheels, cogs and pipes (tin-mining machinery) forms a mound on a rocky seabed at about 16 m. A protected site needing a licence.
sources: Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Maritime Archaeology Society (Virtual Dive Trails)

x-notable-847.name: HMS Royal Anne Galley
x-notable-847.access: Protected wreck (1993): diving by licence only
highlights: Resident grey seals
x-notable-847.summary: Frigate wrecked in 1721 on the rocks off Lizard Point, now a protected wreck in very shallow, exposed water. Only a scatter of guns and objects remains, and diving is by licence.
sources: Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Maritime Archaeology Society

x-notable-849.name: Amsterdam
x-notable-849.reason: Wreck is buried in the Bulverhythe beach, seen only at the lowest tides

x-notable-851.name: U-701
highlights: Largely intact U-boat with 88 mm deck gun
hazards: Shifting sand can bury the wreck; currents vary widely
x-notable-851.summary: A World War II German submarine sunk by aircraft in 1942 and lying largely intact in the shoals off Cape Hatteras. Sand and current decide whether it is visible on a given day, but the deck gun can still be seen when conditions allow.

x-notable-854.name: Erme Ingot Site
x-notable-854.access: Protected wreck; a licence is required to dive on or near it
x-notable-854.summary: Archaeological scatter of tin ingots near West Mary's Rocks off the Erme estuary in Devon, found by divers in 1991-92. A protected wreck site, so only licensed visits are allowed.

x-notable-855.name: HMT Arfon
x-notable-855.access: Designated protected wreck (Protection of Wrecks Act 1973); managed by Historic England
x-notable-855.summary: A WWI naval trawler mined in 1917 and now a protected wreck south of St Alban's Head, lying partly across the tide with the rudder on the seabed near 35 m. Small enough for a no-stop dive yet complex enough to reward more time.

x-notable-856.name: Dunwich Bank Wreck
x-notable-856.access: Protected wreck (Protection of Wrecks Act 1973); diving by licence only
hazards: Almost zero visibility, work by touch
Dive windows only when tidal current eases
x-notable-856.summary: A protected 16th-century wreck mound with bronze guns off Dunwich, Suffolk, in about 15 m. Silty water gives almost no visibility and entry is possible only at slack tide, so work there is by licensed teams.

x-notable-857.name: Chesil Beach cannon
x-notable-857.access: Protected wreck; dive only under a Historic England licence
highlights: Concreted cast-iron cannon, 1650-1725
x-notable-857.summary: Two clusters of concreted 17th to 18th century iron cannon off Chesil Beach, thought to be from separate unidentified wrecks. They are protected sites in 12 to 15 m and can only be dived with a licence.

x-notable-860.name: Wreck site of the Klein Hollandia
highlights: Bronze and iron cannon on the seabed
Hull frames and planking protruding from sand
x-notable-860.summary: A 17th century Dutch warship lying off Eastbourne at about 32 m, protected by law and visited under licence. Divers can see cannon and surviving hull structure, but the depth makes it a planned, demanding dive.
sources: Cultural Heritage Agency of the Netherlands

x-notable-861.name: Yarmouth Roads Wreck
x-notable-861.access: Protected wreck site licensed to the Maritime Archaeology Trust
x-notable-861.summary: The partly buried remains of a 16th century carrack off Yarmouth, Isle of Wight, found in 1984 and now a protected wreck. Only a little timber shows above the seabed, so it is of most interest to heritage-minded divers.

x-notable-862.name: West Bay Wreck
x-notable-862.access: Protected wreck designated under the Protection of Wrecks Act
highlights: Mound of iron bars with a bronze gun
Iron anchor beside the mound
x-notable-862.summary: A small cargo wreck off West Bay in Lyme Bay: a low mound of concreted iron bars with a bronze gun and iron anchor, lying in about 12 m on sand. It is a designated protected wreck site.

x-notable-863.name: Tearing Ledge Wreck
x-notable-863.access: Protected wreck: licence under the Protection of Wrecks Act; licensed Scilly charter boats only
highlights: Heaps of cannon and large iron anchors
hazards: Very strong tides and swell-generated surge
x-notable-863.summary: Remains of a late-17th-century warship on the rocky ledge just south-east of Bishop Rock lighthouse. Divers find piles of iron guns and anchors on a largely kelp-free seabed, in strong tide and surge.
sources: Cornwall and Isles of Scilly Maritime Archaeology Society (Virtual Dive Trails)

x-notable-864.name: Langdon Bay Wreck
hazards: Visibility 2 m or less
x-notable-864.summary: A shallow chalk-bed site off Dover where a Middle Bronze Age cargo of bronze tools and weapons was found by local divers in 1974. It is a protected wreck site with little to see and typically poor visibility.
sources: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record
Kent County Council Historic Environment Record

x-notable-865.name: Moor Sand site
x-notable-865.access: Protected wreck; a licence is required to dive on or near it
x-notable-865.summary: Bronze Age weapons site off Gammon Head in South Devon, found by trainee divers in 1977 and possibly a prehistoric boat's cargo. It is a protected wreck, so diving needs a licence rather than a casual visit.

x-notable-866.name: Studland Bay Wreck
x-notable-866.access: Protected wreck site (Protection of Wrecks Act)
x-notable-866.summary: Scattered remains of an early 16th century merchant ship, found by divers in 1983 near Hook Sands at the mouth of Poole Harbour. Most of the hull is reburied, so little structure is visible.

x-notable-867.name: South Edinburgh Channel Wreck
x-notable-867.reason: Protected wreck reburied under at least six metres of sand; not diveable
sources: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record

x-notable-869.name: HMS Pomone
x-notable-869.access: Protected wreck site licensed to the Maritime Archaeology Trust
highlights: Cannon and carronades strewn on the site
Chalk gullies and ridges with wreck material
hazards: Highly dynamic seabed; dive on slack water
x-notable-869.summary: The scattered remains of a frigate lost on Goose Rock at the Needles in 1811. No hull survives; artefacts lie concreted or wedged in eroded chalk gullies, best visited at slack water on this protected wreck site.

x-notable-876.name: SMS Friedrich der Grosse
x-notable-876.reason: Raised in 1937 and scrapped at Rosyth

x-notable-883.name: HMS Audacious
hazards: Unexploded ordnance around the wreck
Deep: trimix or rebreather diving
x-notable-883.summary: A WWI dreadnought mined in 1914 off Donegal, now resting inverted on the seabed in the open Atlantic. A deep technical dive with often excellent visibility, reached by boat from the Donegal coast.

x-notable-891.name: HMS Pathfinder
x-notable-891.depthNote: Seabed 62 m (one source says 68 m); wreck rises ~8 m
hazards: Ammunition scattered among the wreckage
x-notable-891.summary: The WWI cruiser torpedoed by U-21 lies upright off St Abbs Head, roughly 62-68 m down, and is reported in remarkably good condition. Only suited to technical divers; she is a war grave.

x-notable-894.name: HMS Drake
x-notable-894.summary: Armoured cruiser torpedoed in 1917 and now lying in Church Bay, Rathlin Island. It is a shallow wreck under 20 m in good visibility that can be dived at any state of tide, though salvage has left a scrapyard of plates.

x-notable-902.name: HMS Brazen
highlights: Intact portholes with glass
Guns, torpedo tubes and depth charges
hazards: Tide turns and current builds quickly
x-notable-902.summary: A 1930s destroyer sunk by German aircraft in 1940, lying in roughly 25-30 m east of Dover. Guns, torpedo tubes and depth-charge gear remain, and parts of the hull can be entered, though shifting sand buries and uncovers sections.
sources: Kent County Council Historic Environment Record

x-notable-909.name: SMS Grosser Kurfürst
x-notable-909.reason: Raised in 1938 and scrapped at Rosyth

x-notable-910.name: U-2511
x-notable-910.summary: A Type XXI U-boat scuttled in Operation Deadlight in 1946 and still largely intact in the Atlantic off Donegal. A deep technical wreck at roughly 67-69 m, dived by expedition teams.

x-notable-911.name: U-12
